From 1.20 release, we completely redesigned our old stacked PR model. Instead of mirroring each commits into PRs to make them individually reviewed, merged or abandoned, we just give way flexible diff model. Users can diff between arbitrary commits or interdiff between arbitrary versions. So technically "stacked PR" is gone. Commits are already stacked and giving well-designed interface to view & review it solves most of the scenarios.

But this still leave one limitation: [#216: We can't share same change between PRs.](https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/issues/216)

Many stacked PR implementations including GitHub solves this by literally stacking PRs, creating dependency graph, letting each branches to *depend* (*be stacked*) on others. Apart from the fact that we can't really follow same solution because tangled PRs are detached from their source branch by design, I also think that isn't really good way to do this. We already have commit DAG. Building similar DAG between branches on top of that makes everything hard to understand and super complicated.

Instead, we can literally share changes between PRs and make that clear. Same direction we took for 1.20 PR system redesign; expose internal model clearly with fine interface.

To achieve this, we should show these informations on PR page:

- On commit row: other PRs including this commit in their latest submission range
- On commit row: whether this commit is already merged into target branch (related: [#4734](https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/issues/4734))
- On discussion section: comments made from other PR but pinned to same jj-change

This needs some UI research before we proceed. I'm not sure if it's possible to build such interface and if it really solves the problem at all.

title.text: Track commits across PRs by change-id (tangled stacked PR)

As an alternative option to this, would be great to use git trailers instead of modifying the user generated commit for this. Adding (#23) to squash commits is something that GitHub has gotten "wrong" for many years. In the sense that we accept it, but only as the least bad of the options when you want a neat linear history that doesn't fight the tooling all the way.

I still think doing the github style squash is a good thing to have for compatibility with existing systems, but it's worth considering approaches that solve the problem better. A trailer would more naturally be an id that survives moving source control systems as it references the actual system and not just an relative id. Just think about your repos that you're migrating from github to tangled and what #23 means in all your historic commits.

body.text:
ADR 5 makes the iOS app an untrusted public atproto OAuth client. The atproto OAuth spec says such clients should get sessions and refresh tokens limited to 2 weeks, while confidential clients may have unlimited sessions with 180-day refresh tokens (https://atproto.com/specs/oauth, "Tokens and Session Lifetime"). The two-week limit is accepted for the first release.

The spec also allows a mobile app and a token-mediating backend to form one confidential client ("Types of Clients"). This issue tracks evaluating that as the way to longer sessions: the crate server would hold the client signing key and authenticate token and refresh requests, while the DPoP key stays in the device's Secure Enclave.

Questions to settle:

- Can token requests be mediated without the server ever holding the tokens, or does it see them in transit?
- Does every refresh then depend on crate being reachable, and what happens offline?
- Key rotation and revocation through the advertised JWKS for an app-plus-backend client.
- Whether real users actually hit the two-week re-login often enough to justify it.

title.text: Evaluate a token-mediating backend for longer iOS OAuth sessions
